list.listitem: Abstinence from tobacco and limited alcohol intake (ie, 8 oz wine, 2 cans beer) is recommended. C

Leukoplakia should be followed carefully. If changes in thickness or development of inflammation after 14 days, recommend biopsy. Lesions that subside with removal of irritant are almost certainly benign. C
Persistent erythroplasia should be biopsied. C
If lesions prove to be severe dysplasia, carcinoma in situ, or invasive carcinoma, evaluate the upper aerodigestive tract for multiple primary lesions. C
Oral leukoplakia or erythroplasia without evidence of severe dysplasia or invasive malignancy is generally treated with carbon dioxide or other laser or surgical excision. C

Perform careful visual examination for erythroplastic lesions in the high-risk sites in high-risk groups, such as smokers and drinkers, and in patients with a previous aerodigestive squamous carcinoma. C

background.definition: Leukoplakia appears as a white keratotic lesion on the mucosal surface. It is related to the presence of a physical or chemical irritant. If there is no associated inflammatory component, it is unlikely to be an omen of developing carcinoma. Erythroplasia is an inflammatory manifestation due to the submucosal angiogenic vascular and lymphohistiocytic response to genetic alterations, severe dysplasia, carcinoma in situ, or early invasive carcinoma. There are two distinct types of erythroplasia that suggest carcinoma. The first is a granular, red velvety lesion with stippled or patchy areas of normal mucosa or keratin within or peripheral to the lesion. Usually, the mucosa is not ulcerated, but may be "heaped up." The other is a smooth, nongranular lesion, primarily red and inflammatory with minimal or no keratosis.

list.listitem: Leukoplakia: variable incidence in general population depending on gender and location; 409/100,000 per year in men and 70/100,000 per year in women in Japan, 240/100,000 per year in men and 3/100,000 per year in women in India (related to the betel nut). Most commonly found in patients between the ages of 50 and 70 years and users of smokeless tobacco.

Erythroplasia is most often found in middle-aged and elderly patients who are consistent daily drinkers and smokers. Occasionally, elderly women and a subset of patients between the ages of 20 and 30 years with no apparent risk factors have erythroplasia. Erythroplasia is not as common as leukoplakia but is more worrisome as an indicator of significant dysplastic pathology.
Leukoplakia: older studies have shown a 1.5% to 4.3% prevalence of leukoplakia in the general population. A recent decrease in prevalence has been reported: 0.66% in men, 0.21% in women; 0.42% total.

Erythroplasia: much less common than leukoplakia but invariably present with early carcinoma in situ or carcinoma. Erythroplasia was seen in 93% of 236 early invasive oral/oropharyngeal (O/OP) carcinoma cases and 94% of 90 carcinoma in situ cases.

A systematic review of the prevalence of oral potentially malignant disorders found an overall prevalence of 4.5%. They were more common in men than women, and in Asian and South American/Caribbean populations.

A review of 50 years of data from University of California San Francisco database of oral potentially malignant disorders found a risk of malignant transformation of 50% in those with erythroplakia, higher if also smokers. This compared to 8.4% risk of transformation for leukoplakia and 5% risk for submucous fibrosis.

Leukoplakia appears to be a protective response to physical and chemical irritants (or other unknown etiologies). Various forms of tobacco and other chronic irritants are believed to cause keratinized lesions. Chronic irritation from dentures, sharp teeth, hot or spicy foods, and other physical agents may play a role. On occasion, a homogenous leukoplakic lesion may exhibit dysplasia and the red inflammatory component is obscured by the keratin.

Erythroplasia is a submucosal angiogenic vascular and lymphohistiocytic response to the genetic changes in the squamous cells. It is strongly associated with consistent daily drinking and smoking; human papillomavirus is also a possible etiology.

Leukoplakia is a keratinized response to the nonkeratinized O/OP mucosa. The white color may result from hydration of the keratin of the normal nonkeratinized mucosa rather than the increased thickness of the stratum corneum per se. It appears to be a protective mechanism.
Erythroplasia is an inflammatory submucosal (angiogenesis and immune) response to the change in genetic pattern of the squamous cells of the overlying mucosa.
Abstinence from tobacco and moderation of alcohol intake is the best prevention. C

There are no clinical trials comparing annual screening to no screening and a single RCT suggesting survival benefit from visual examination screeening was of low quality and not considered conclusive with current USPSTF recommendation that screening is not warranted on present evidence.C

A 25 year population-based study of patients with oral lichen planus concluded that they had a 5-fold increased relative risk of developing oral squamous cancer, suggesting a potential benefit to monitoring these patients over the longer term.

A Cochrane review of 14 studies and 909 patients addressed whether interventions in leukoplakia might reduce development of oral cancer. The evidence available was of low quality with no clear indication for effective preventative therapy.

Consider adding to routine examinations a careful visual examination for erythroplastic lesions in the high-risk sites (floor of the mouth, ventrolateral tongue, soft palate, anterior and posterior tonsillar pillars, and the lingual aspect of the retromolar trigone) in high-risk groups (ie, smokers and drinkers) and in patients with a previous squamous cell carcinoma. C
In spite of large numbers of subjects in observational studies, the efficacy of green tea in cancer prevention remains unproven.

Leukoplakia may persist 14 days after removal of the irritant or suspected cause. If the lesions appear thickened or irregular, or have developed inflammation, refer for further evaluation and possible biopsy. C
Asymptomatic erythroplasia in high-risk sites (the floor of the mouth, ventrolateral tongue, and soft-palate complex) should be considered invasive carcinoma or carcinoma in situ and biopsied. C
If an erythroplastic lesion is identified, evaluate the pharynx, larynx, hypopharynx, and lungs to rule out the presence of multiple primary cancers. C

A standardized protocol should be applied for O/OP lesions with a proper understanding of the implications of leukoplakia and erythroplasia. A routine screening examination is fairly sensitive and specific for detecting oral cancer or precancer.
Document smoking and drinking history, medication use, and any systemic factors that induce mucosal changes.

Perform a careful visual examination for erythroplastic lesions in the high-risk sites (floor of the mouth, ventrolateral tongue, soft palate, anterior and posterior tonsillar pillars, and lingual aspect of the retromolar trigone).

Identify leukoplakia as white keratotic patches without a visual inflammatory component that cannot be scrapped off. If leukoplakia is found, remove acute or chronic irritants, such as chewing tobacco or dental appliances, and re-examine in 10 to 14 days. If leukoplakia is still present, refer patient for assessment and possible biopsy.

Identify erythroplasia as a red inflammatory lesion with or without keratosis. If erythroplasia is found, refer patient for biopsy. Also, if an O/OP erythroplastic lesion is identified, evaluate the pharynx, larynx, hypopharynx, and lungs to rule out the presence of multiple primary cancers.

The color of a lesion is important. Redness is a color component of most early invasive carcinomas: most early invasive carcinomas are only red (32%), mostly red with some white (32%), or equal parts red and white (23%). Only 12% are mostly or only white.
Refer all patients with erythroplasia, nonresolving leukoplakia, or questionable oral lesions for further evaluation and/or biopsy by an oral and maxillofacial surgeon or an otolaryngologist.

Research has suggested that toluidine blue (TB) solution, a metachromatic nuclear stain can serve as a diagnostic adjunct to a visual O/OP cancer examination. TB clinically stains malignant mucosal lesions, but not normal mucosa. Although the appropriate use of TB results in few false-negative results, it must be stressed that sound clinical suspicion mandates biopsy regardless of staining outcome.
Look for leukoplakia and erythroplasia during all oral examinations.

Leukoplakia and any inflammation present caused by trauma or irritation will usually improve after 10 to 14 days. Uniformly white lesions, consistent with leukoplakia, are invariably benign, unless, in rare instances, keratinization masks the red inflammation.
Biopsy is required for all erythroplasia, even the most minimal, that persists without apparent cause for 10 to 14 days.
A biopsy should be performed for all lesions with unknown etiology.
Once a lesion is visually diagnosed and persistent, refer the patient to an appropriate practitioner for biopsy and management. C

Treatment is determined by lesion size: Lesions smaller than 2 cm are usually excised, those larger than 2 cm are surgically removed and/or receive radiation therapy, and all lesions with cervical metastases get adjunct radiation therapy. C
Complications are more likely to result from an erroneous diagnosis and by waiting for changes to occur over prolonged periods. C

If you confirm severe dysplasia, carcinoma in situ, or early invasive carcinoma by biopsy, and the lesion is 2 cm or smaller, perform wide local excision. If the lesion is larger than 2 cm, surgery or radiotherapy is indicated.

If cervical metastases are diagnosed, surgery and radiotherapy for the neck are standard modalities. There is no evidence that elective neck dissection in early stage patients improves overall outcome.
Radiation therapy can be used for lesions larger than 2 cm in diameter or with cervical metastases.
Combined chemotherapy and radiation therapy are also used, depending on pathology and metastases.

A 2021 updated Cochrane review examined the role of chemotherapy in oral cavity/oropharyngeal malignancy with 100 trials and over 18,000 patients. They concluded that chemotherapy offers benefit in survival when combined with locoregional therapy, given with radiotherapy after surgery, or with radiotherapy as primary treatment. There was no evidence for benefit from chemotherapy alone as induction treatment, though.

Oral leukoplakia or erythroplasia without evidence of severe dysplasia or invasive malignancy is generally treated with carbon dioxide or other laser, cryoprobe, or with surgical excision. However, adequately powered randomized trials are lacking.
Topical 5-aminolevulinic acid (5-ALA) photodynamic therapy has been proposed as a less invasive alternative for the treatment of oral leukoplakia, but has not been well studied.
For erythroplasia or persistent leukoplakia, refer patients for evaluation and/or biopsy by an oral and maxillofacial surgeon or an otolaryngologist.

If asymptomatic erythroplasia or leukoplakia is proved by biopsy to be squamous cell carcinoma, especially less than 2 cm in diameter without cervical node metastasis, prognosis for survival is excellent. B
Leukoplakia rarely transforms into malignancy unless accompanied by erythroplasia (red inflammation). Leukoplakias develop into cancer at very low frequencies over a prolonged period.
Many of the recorded conversions to cancer are of lesions that had erythroplastic components described as leukoplakia.
Persistent erythroplasia, with or without the white component, in high-risk sites should be considered squamous cell carcinoma until proven otherwise.

Risk factors for progression of oral potentially malignant disorders to malignancy include size >200 mm2, nonhomogeneous texture, red or speckled color, location on the tongue or floor of the mouth, female sex, age over 50 years, and non-smoker.
The prognosis for survival is excellent if asymptomatic erythroplasia or leukoplakia is proved by biopsy to be carcinoma. These lesions are usually 2 cm or smaller.
The color of a lesion is important. Most invasive carcinomas are only red (32%), mostly red with some white (32%), or equal parts red and white (23%). Only 12% are mostly or only white.
Leukoplakia should be followed up clinically. Most will resolve within 14 days if the causative irritant, such as chewing tobacco or a dental appliance, is removed.

When the irritant is not removed (for example, a patient with persistent use of chewing tobacco), follow-up clinically and biopsy any change in appearance, development of an inflammatory component, or increase in size.
Stop using all tobacco products, including chewing tobacco.
Limit alcohol use to no more than 8 ounces of wine, 2 oz of liquor, or 2 cans of beer daily.
